The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On schedule I:
Customs tariff-415b.	Washing machines,
domestic, with or without motive power incorporated therein; complete parts of washing machines: 25 per cent.

I was speaking on this item the other evening when the committee adjourned, two or three minutes before the six o'clock hour. I would have finished had I been given the opportunity. The item was not carried. I have no wish to embarrass the minister, but I want to lay some facts before him and his tariff experts regarding the use of electricity in various forms of equipment which has grown out of the rapid expansion of the hydroelectric industry in Ontario. For example, we have item 415a-which was not carried- refrigerators, domestic or store, completely equipped or not; one is electric, the second is other than electric. The other evening the minister gave some explanation of this particular item, and I just wish to refer for three or four minutes-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I would remind the hon. member that the item under consideration is 415b.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The same thing. It is all right.
The item, (a) as I understand it, is refrigerators.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, washing machines.

We might as well not carry on at all if a member cannot ask a question of the government. It is all the

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
same item. The government is not objecting to this. What are we here for? Regarding these refrigerators, washing machines and sewing machines, I put down a resolution, at the opening of parliament, regarding these matters, and asked what the tariff board was doing about the cost of the various items of equipment referred to it, and we heard that they had not had a sitting for very nearly a year. Then they met.
As has been said, there has been a rapid expansion of this industry. Prior to 1935 the tariff was forty per cent. Under the agreement in 1935 with the United States it came down to thirty-five per cent. Immediately imports from the United States went up, and the figures I have show that they increased from $189,000 to $893,000, or five times as much as they were before. The point I wish to raise, and I might just as well finish in one short speech what I have to say with reference to five or six of these items which relate to all kinds of electric equipment, is this. We have in Canada 42,000,000 horse-power, only one-sixth of which, or seven million, is developed, and some of that only for part of the year. This is a new and struggling industry, applying direct current for the use of all kinds of household equipment, and getting the benefit of cheap power for domestic use. Formerly a large part of the electrical equipment now manufactured in Canada came from Germany, but the industry for years made, and is making, a great effort to establish itself in this country by a little protection. It is a struggling industry, only in its infancy, and I submit that everything possible should be done to encourage it with a view to providing more employment. I realize quite well how desirable it is that housewives and people generally should be enabled to make use of electrical power at low cost for equipment and service in their homes for refrigerators, washing machines and other necessary devices. It is in the interests of the consumers that these things should be provided at reasonable cost, but at the same time I trust that the employment feature and the need of helping home industries will not be overlooked by the government. Rapid strides are being made in the extension of the use of electricity in connection with medicine, health, and all kinds of home comforts, and in other lines, and I do suggest that the government should help to put the industry on its feet and expand it. We cannot visualize the extended use of electricity in the future in the kitchen and in other parts of the house and domestic industry. I have figures which I could submit to the committee but I am
afraid it would not be possible to give them at this stage. This industry is operating in Hamilton, Peterborough and other parts of Canada, and the figures which the minister gave the other evening will show its importance.
Our imports of electrical refrigerators alone from the United States, for the last year, were $950,000 and of other refrigerators $245,000. The numbers imported from the United States were 14,894, and 4,049 respectively. We exported 7,000, our largest customer being Australia with the United Kingdom second. These figures alone show what can be done in this industry not only in connection with refrigerators, but in the production of other electrical equipment as well. The electrical equipment industry is in its infancy and with proper development it could be made a fertile source of employment. The use of electricity will in the future be applied in fields of activity which at present we do not visualize, providing employment for Canadian workmen, and assisting in production and distribution and agriculture. The member for Victoria-Carleton referred to this subject the other evening. There is no doubt a demand on the part of the public to have these inventions made available at cost plus a reasonable profit, and I suggest that the minister should have someone, either in his office or in the office of the tariff board, determine a price that would allow a reasonable profit to the manufacturers and at the same time promote production at reasonable cost in Canada and thus help employment. I hope there will be no further reductions until this great industry is well established, because I am sure it could be made to provide employment for thousands of Canadians in the provinces that use commercial and domestic power extensively as well as throughout the dominion in the use of domestic electrical equipment.

I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Finance to the price of washing machines. In my opinion this is an item that should be referred to the tariff board. Last summer I made inquiries regarding comparative prices in the United States and Canada, and I also investigated the small combination gasoline engine and washing machine. There are only two or three companies in the United States that make these small gasoline engines, which work perfectly with washing machines. We have to import them. The duty under this item is 25 per cent, but I can state on reliable authority that a better washing machine can be bought in the United States at half the price we have to pay in Manitoba. That difference of
2172	COMMONS
Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
100 per -cent is too much money. We have no objection to a certain amount of tariff protection for the benefit of Canadian workmen, but 100 per cent is altogether too much. I should be glad to have the item referred to the tariff board.

I note that there is a 20 per cent British preferential tariff, and 25 per cent United States. Will the minister give the imports from Great Britain and from the United States? Perhaps he can also give us the figures covering the total quantities manufactured in Canada in 1938.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There were no imports; from Great Britain; in fact we export washing machines to Great Britain. The imports from the United States amounted to $702,000-last year.
If I may say a word in reply to the two hon. members from Manitoba who have spoken, I would say that the record before me shows that there has been quite an increase-in the imports of washing machines since the 1935 agreement, which, it will be remembered, reduced the duty from 35 per cent to 25 per cent. With the coming into full operation of this agreement the present effective rate of 28 per cent, including excise tax,, will of course be reduced to 25 per cent. But I call attention to the fact that during: the three years 1936 to 1938 inclusive, imports did increase from $272,000 to $702,000. They trebled in value. The number of machines-imported increased five-fold during that period. I shall, however, take note of the-representations that have been made suggesting that a tariff board inquiry might be desirable. I do not undertake that such a reference will be made, but the matter will' be looked into from that point of view. At the present time we have quite an export business; exports have grown as rapidly as; the imports. Last year we exported a total of $1,481,000 worth of washing machines, the great bulk of which went to the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand. I shall take note of the suggestions made by my hon. friends and find out what the facts are.

The statement of the % minister that a reference in this matter might, be made to the tariff board impels me to say that while I have all the sympathy in the-world with the representations made by the two hon. members who have spoken on the-subject, there is another side to the story to which I think I should refer. If a reference-is made to the tariff board, obviously both sides will be heard.
The washing machine industry in the United States is not in a prosperous condition. As far as the story can be gathered from the financial reports of these companies -there are not many of them, but their output is very large-it is not a very attractive one. As a result some of these companies; are actually dumping machines in Canada in order to keep up production and keep down the overhead ratio. That at any rate is what is claimed, and I think there is sufficient evidence to support that view. Briefly stated, the washing machine manufacturers of the United States produced in 1938 about 1,200,000 washers. Yet it is clear from their annual statements, some of which I have seen,.

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
and from information which I consider to be reliable, that the industry not only did not make any money but lost heavily. For instance the Automatic Electric Washer Company, of Newton, Iowa, producing about 30,000 machines a year, in their report showed a loss of $105,000, or approximately $3.50 per machine.
It might also be pointed out that these companies have different grades of machines. They put out a higher priced machine, which is the most profitable type, and which they seek to sell in their own market; and besides that they produce a low priced machine which they can feature in their advertisements to attract buyers. Most of these companies limit the number of low priced machines to a small percentage of their output. I understand the large General Electric Company limit the number of low priced machines to fifteen per cent of their total output. These low priced machines are used as loss leaders. It is also reported that the Easy Washing Machine Company, a well known company over there, lost something in the neighbourhood of $400,000 last year. Their annual production is about 200,000 machines. They make a range of machines selling from $49 to $150.
Another feature of this operation was referred to a moment ago, the attachments, such as electric motors and the tubs, which are usually manufactured separately. It is reported that the manufacturers of washing machine tubs lost on an average about fifty cents a tub last year, and the manufacture of the motors is also reported to have shown a loss.
The Washing Machine Company of Fairfield, Iowa, make a machine selling at $39, but they limit the production of those machines to one hundred a year; and while the company advertise machines ranging in price from $39 up to $100 or whatever the top price may be, the salesmen would be pretty severely taken to task if they placed many of those $39 machines. They are told they can show it, but to advise the purchase of a higher class machine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the company produced only one hundred, they would not be of much use for any purpose.

No, except for advertising-that they make a machine at that price. But the salesmen were instructed that their efficiency' would be judged by the small number of that class of machine that they placed.
A further point is that certain of these machines have been shipped into Canada at an invoice price of $24.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Out of the hundred?

Well, there may have been some of that class. As near as can be ascertained, these machines cost about $34.
I do not say it in any critical sense, but one of the questions which ought to be examined is whether there has not been systematic dumping of lower priced machines on the Canadian market, tending to destroy the industry here.
There is another aspect of this matter which should also be remembered. Usually these low priced machines are in the long run more costly than the higher priced machines-not those at the highest prices, but those moderately priced. A machine selling at what we might call a normal price will usually last a considerable time, being fairly well made, so that the actual annual outlay by the purchaser is comparatively small. Of course they are usually sold on time.
While I am entirely in accord with the view that we should secure for the users of this class of household utensil as low a price as we possibly can, yet in the interest of common sense and the welfare of the industrialists of Canada, which after all is very important, we must not allow ourselves to become the victims of a sort of "loss leader" dumping practice on the part of our friends south of the line. The evidence is pretty clear that the industry in that country has been in a somewhat unprofitable condition for the last few years, and because of that fact there has been a tendency to slash prices.
I think there is one thing that can be definitely said for the Canadian manufacturers of washing machines, that as far as I know-and I know some of them-they have all been putting out excellent machines, supplying the Canadian market at reasonable prices. The value of this industry, together with similar industries, is undoubtedly great, and I must repeat what has been said by some other hon. members during the last two or three weeks in discussing these resolutions as well as in connection with other matters, that after all the value of the industrial market to the farmer is important. I would suggest to my hon. friends who advanced the argument a few moments ago, that the real approach to the problem of the farmers is to secure for them a fair price for their products, which they are not getting to-day. That is my confirmed opinion. I think we will have a much healthier economic condition among the farmers of Canada if we can devise a system under which we can stabilize at a fair level the prices received by the farmers for their products, and I am now speaking particularly of live stock, dairy products and, of course, all grains.

Would the hon. member inform us what method he would follow in order to attain that end?

I think such a dissertation now would be out of order, but I am not unmindful of the point and am quite prepared to express my views at the proper time, because I have given the question a great deal of thought. At the moment I am merely giving, shall I say, the other side of the story, which we must constantly bear in mind. It would not be fair to put the minister in a position in which in a sense he would be resisting an appeal in the interests of the farmers of Canada, which is virtually the position in which he was placed. As far as I am concerned I certainly wish to uphold the demands of agriculture for better and fairer treatment, yet nothing is gained by glossing over the other side of the picture or, merely for the sake of some momentary encomiums from that quarter, neglecting to tell what are the facts. So I suggest to the minister that when the matter goes to the tariff board-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say it would.
If and when it goes to the tariff board, both sides of the story should be heard.

There have been a number of items upon which I should have liked to say a word, but since this one has aroused some discussion I want to support those who have suggested that such articles as washing machines should be referred for investigation to the tariff board, or that something definite should be done by the government to reduce the duty. If an investigation of this kind be undertaken, I suggest to the minister that since we export a considerable number of these machines to Great Britain, a comparison should be made between the prices of such articles in Great Britain and in Canada. There may be very little difference, but sometimes on picking up English publications we find articles with which we are familiar in Canada advertised at prices which seem to be in line with our own prices or sometimes even a little less.
As one who occasionally passes through the United States I must say that I do not know of any group of articles upon which the differential appears to be as great as between the two sides of the line as electrical appliances and articles of this description. What the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) has said may be quite true, but I have always been struck by the tremendous difference between the prices of refrigerators, electrical appliances, washing machines and so on. Some twelve or thirteen years ago we

bought a washing machine made in the United States, for which we paid something in the neighbourhood of $160. In store windows across the line I saw the very same machine for sale at less than $100. That struck me at the time as being a tremendous difference in price.
While it is true that the manufacture of such articles means work for those engaged in Canadian factories, I sometimes wonder whether we are not paying far too great a price for the work that is distributed by industries of this description. I think if an industry is uneconomic and is robbing, as it were, a large consuming public in this country, it has no right to receive special consideration.
Would wheat come under that?

No; wheat does not
come under that, for reasons which we shall probably discuss within the course of the next few days.	*
To-day throughout Canada there are thousands of people who lack many simple household utensils. Very many articles have been discussed in connection with this treaty which cause me to say that we should do everything we can to bring into effect what after all is the Liberal policy, as stated over and over again in the program of the Liberal party ever since 1919; that is, to remove the protective tariff from articles which are necessary to the general welfare of the family. I am rising simply to give perhaps still another side of the picture and to suggest to the minister that he give consideration to the request of the two hon. members from Manitoba who have spoken.

I am quite certain
that everyone in what is commonly called the rump, as well as those on the main street of the Liberal party, will accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) that we should do everything possible to safeguard the industrial producer and the industrial worker in the Dominion of Canada. But there is some variation of opinion as to what constitutes the best method of helping him. The items we have been discussing recently concern largely iron and steel. I am not particularly interested in this individual item, but looking at the matter from a broad national standpoint I am anxious that the iron and steel industry in Canada should prosper. I looked up the figures in order to see what we have been doing in the last few years, and I bring a message of cheer not only to the hon. member for Kootenay East but to all those on my immediate left who are particularly interested in this problem.

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
In 1933 our production of iron and steel products was 8211,000,000. Those figures have increased year by year. The following year they were $308,000,000, and in the year the Liberals came into office and started to "ruin the industry" they were $390,000,000. The following year they were $453,000,000 and the next year $623,000,000. I do not hear a word of cheer from my friends to my left, although from time to time they have told us that the approach of the Liberal party to office always meant the retreat of industry.
Let me deal with wages, which, in my opinion is a very important factor. They moved up from $69,000,000 in 1933 to $88,000,000 and then to $110,000,000. We, the Liberals, arrived on the scene, and the figures were $126,000,000, $164,000,000-and still the cheering opposition army is silent; nothing but criticism! Then, how many men were employed? In 1933 there were 70,000; then 81,000, 95,000, 107,000; and the army of workers who marched into the iron and steel factories of Canada in 1937 numbered 127,336. Leaving out war years, that level was never touched, except in one year, 1929.
In 1929 production of iron and steel products stood at $738,000,000. We have not equalled that figure so far, but we are closely approaching it, with the $623,000,000 of 1937. In addition it must be remembered that there was, or should have been in the period of 3'ears from 1929 to 1937, at least to some extent a decline in price levels. So that if we could make the comparison on the basis of actual volume, rather than value, we would see that we have almost approached the highest limit we have ever reached in any peace year.
I should like to touch upon another item. My hon. friends are always afraid of imports. Well, in the year in which imports were shut out to the greatest extent, that is in the year 1933, when they fell to a value of $58,000,000, we were producing only to a value of $211,000,000. In 1937 we were importing goods to the value of $150,000,000 and producing them to a value of $623,000,000. So that it seems that as imports grow, so also does production; and industry moves forward as we break down the barriers, just as will the other sections of production in Canada.
The hon. member for Kootenay East referred to dumping. I think someone should offer a prize for the production of a genuine case of proved dumping. I sat and listened before the tariff board, year after year to- I forget how many cases, it must have been about two hundred-and I heard charges and counter-charges made in regard to dumping. The only cases I can recall which seemed reasonably clearly proved were ones in which 71492-137
Canadian manufacturers were exporting abroad at prices lower than they charged at home. No one offers to bring forward the evidence, but when you want to paint the picture of dumping it is the easiest thing in the world, if you are inclined that way, to splash on a ten-league canvas, with brushes of comets' hair. But, after all, if we are going to extend industry in Canada it must be brought about by bringing the products we produce within the capacity of the people of Canada to purchase.
I am quite interested in the statement of the hon. member for Kootenay East. Price policies and production have been clearly discussed in a recent book put out by the Brookings Institution of Washington. I ordered a few copies the other day, and out of kindness to my hon. friend, and the high regard 1 have for him not only because of his interest in this but in other problems, and in his to-day professed interest-I know it is real- in agriculture, I propose to make him a present of a copy of the book, in the hope that he may be converted to that point of view, and that I may have the pleasure of saving at least one brand from the burning.
May I bring the committee back to the item under discussion.

I know they increased.
We would not be able to export at all if we were not able to manufacture for our own market. We would be able to export more if we had the whole of our own market. But I wish to point out that according to the figures supplied by the washing machine industry, 309 fewer men were engaged in the industry in Canada in 1936 than in 1935.

It has been suggested by the hon. member for Souris, and to some extent by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Furniss) that washing machines were selling in Canada at twice the price at which they were selling in the United States. The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) suggested that they were being dumped into Canada. Now, if they are being dumped into Canada one would think that they were being sold in this country at a price lower than that at which they were selling in the United States. The two views conflict. Both conditions can hardly prevail.
It has been suggested that there is such a duty on washing machines that they are being sold at an excessive price in Canada. The hon. member for Kootenay East quoted figures which indicated that companies in the United States had lost money. I believe if that point were followed out he would find that, generally speaking, the washing machine companies in Canada also lost money last year. There might be an exception here and there, but, generally speaking, the washing machine industry last year was not productive of profit. There are a considerable number of companies in Canada making washing machines, so that there is a good deal of competition in our own country. There is competition among the companies themselves, and that naturally keeps the price down. No company in Canada has what one might call a monopoly.
It has been suggested by several hon. members that this matter should be referred to the tariff board. My opinion is that at the present time we must give industry confidence. We should let them know that they are going to be allowed to carry on their business, without too much interference from governments or other authorities. I would say that this great industry is not one which should be scrutinized by any board. It should be

given an opportunity to conduct its business free, from interference. If that is done I am satisfied that the people will get their washing machines at a fair price.
It has been said that we want to get washing machines as cheaply as possible, and I agree with that; the women on the farms and the mothers and housewives in our cities should get these machines as cheaply as possible. But if we are going to destroy this industry, if it is put out of business and all these machines are to be brought in from a foreign country, I ask where the husbands of the housewives are going to get the money with which to buy them? I submit that we must consider the whole question of industry. Are we going to encourage industry in this country or are we going to destroy industry and create more unemployment? Our one thought should be to be fair to all, to give our housewives whether living in the city or on the farm, washing machines at a fair price; 'but at the same time we should protect this industry and keep our working men at work.

I want to congratulate my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald), who is a neighbour of mine, upon his protectionist speech. Every time an item in this trade treaty is discussed and hon. members refer to the price they have to pay, they refer to the retail price. Member after member has risen to condemn industry. Our manufacturers have 'been called profiteers and hon. members complain of the high prices they have to pay for commodities. But it is not industry that is making the money out of these things. Take washing machines, for instance. If you follow the price of a washing machine from the factory until it reaches the consumer you will find that thirty, thirty-five, forty and forty-five per cent has been added to the price received by the manufacturer. Surely it would be better to spend our time in trying to work out some method of cutting down the cost of distribution in this country than to criticize industry day after day as it has been criticized. I agree with the hon. member for Brantford, when he says that industry should have some assurance that it will not be continually interfered with. Industry certainly has no such assurance now.

the building back in 1921 of the large unit of the John Inglis Company Limited it was difficult to have these heavy units of machinery made in Canada. They equipped that very expensive plant to turn and twist, as it were, steel sheets as heavy as seven-eighths thickness. The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) will realize that that is an extremely heavy sheet to stay-bolt and roll and make into heavy machinery. Since they were unable to compete with similar plants in the United States, and since the demand in Canada during the depression was not so heavy, that plant finally went out of existence.
I use that as an illustration of the type of plant which has gone out of existence or has very considerably reduced its production. The same is true of a plant at Galt, one at Montreal, and one out Welland way: they all experienced the same difficulty. But the point I want to bring out is rather in contradiction of what we heard a few moments ago from the hon. member for Huron North. In departing from the Fielding idea of a revenue tariff as I heard that minister explain it on many occasions from the government side of the house, they have reduced the duties to a very low level, as low in this case as -ten per cent on goods of a class or kind not made in Canada. The result is that plants of this kind, if presented with a blueprint of a heavy type of machinery which is not produced here, are discouraged by the fact that the tariff is only ten per cent, whereas if they were in production on that kind of machine the duty would be 25 per cent. Every time you enlarge the spread between machinery of a kind that is made in Canada and machinery of a kind that is generally not made in Canada, you lose the revenue from tariffs-imposed on a principle which as I have always understood is part and parcel of the policy of the Liberal party, That is the first thing that happens. Secondly, you restrict the possibility of our manufacturers in the iron and steel industry producing that unit of machinery. By the way, industries such as the John Inglis Company did almost as much business, in dollar value, in machinery specially designed as in ordinary boiler shop work.

a great many of our present industries who diversify their manufacture of machinery of this kind could keep their staffs busy designing and building these machines.
The committee realizes that in any industry the machinery changes every two or three years. The ordinary half-million dollar plant would have $200,000 worth of machinery, and it cannot be used for ten years because something more modern and efficient keeps coming up all the time and the old machinery has to be scrapped and modem equipment installed. These new machines are produced in the large countries such as the United States, some in England and some on the continent; so that the Canadian manufacturer may be producing a machine called by one name to-day, which is replaced by a machine called by another name to-morrow, which is doing the work far more efficiently and quickly, with the result that the manufacturer has to throw out the old machine at present made in Canada and bring in the new unit not made here. If the same principle were adopted for collection of these duties on articles imported purely for domestic consumption it would make a great deal of difference in the price and would enable many consumers to obtain articles they cannot now afford because of the spread that exists between United States and Canadian prices.

I think it should be made clear to the hon. member that in regard to the sales tax, the customs tariff and the excise tax, these are all pyramided, and there is an increase added as they move along. The sales tax collected at the factory door goes into the cost of the goods. The merchant takes those goods at a cost which represents the sales tax plus the invoice value of the goods and adds his mark-up. In consequence our eight per cent sales tax is reflected in an added cost amounting to probably twelve per cent, while a forty per cent duty probably runs up to a sixty or seventy per cent advance in the cost of the commodity to the consumer. So pyramid is piled on pyramid, and that is the fundamental reason why the spread between the prices of certain commodities in the United States and Canada is so great. We have to add the duty, or the manufacturer takes it in excess prices; then we must add a series of profits until we have reached such heights that a revulsion of feeling is caused. Then, when we want to bring it down, the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) offers objection.

I have had sent to me a

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
they will be able to speak intelligently in regard to the matter. The statement is from the Detroit Free Press of March 19, and is contained in a dispatch dated at Ottawa, March 18. Perhaps the easiest way is to read part of it. It is supposed to be a statement of fact. The gist of the statement is that of the three large automobile manufacturing companies in Canada, at least two are on the verge of closing down because of the change in duties, and the cutting off of the excise tax of three per cent. I shall read a paragraph. If the minister wishes me to stop reading it, I shall do so. It is not meant as a criticism, but it can be placed before the committee better by reading it than could be done by an attempt to synopsize it. This is a special dispatch to the Detroit Free Press, dated Ottawa, March 18. It reads:
The Canadian government, it is learned on high authority, is concentrating on the problem of preventing the largest branch plant industry operated by United States capital in Canada- the automobile industry-from being lost to the dominion and repatriated to the United States.
Of the "big three" motor car manufacturers who maintain complete plants in Canada, one alone is described in governmental circles as being content to remain in the dominion.
The other two are said to be anxious to discontinue their Canadian operations and to transfer the substantial volume of employment that they afford to their parent factories in the United States, where enlarged mass production methods would effect important savings.
Lower down it states:
The new Canada-United States trade treaty is responsible directly for the critical situation. The arrangement binds at 17i per cent the duty payable on United States automobiles coming into Canada and removes the three per cent excise tax which has been required on motor cars imported into Canada from any country other than Great Britain in recent years.
Then the article goes on to emphasize the importance to the automobile industry of the loss of this three per cent, and gives further details of the advantages to automobile companies of importing their cars instead of manufacturing them in Canada. The article continues :
When Canadian officials discovered that the new trade treaty threatened to have this effect on one of the country's most important industries, they formulated representations to Washington.
I am just trying to give the gist of this article. Lower down it says:
The proposal w-as made, accordingly, that three companies should be approached to write President Roosevelt in support of the Canadian application for a change in the treaty.
Conferences, however, speedily made it apparent that the United States automobile manufacturers were not favourably inclined.

And again:
The suggestion most commonly heard is that the Minister of National Revenue, J. L. Ilsley, takes advantage of a section of the Customs Act which empowers him to declare special duties on commodities that are being "dumped" on the Canadian market.
This is a fairly long article and I think I have read enough to give the gist. It was sent to me by one of the automobile workers' associations. The hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Brown) has had the same thing sent to him and, I believe, will have something to say about it later on because it directly affects his constituency. I should like to hear what they have to say in regard to it.

Before the minister answers the leader of the opposition, may I say that for the past several days I have been receiving hundreds of communications from people in my riding in reference to this matter. I shall not attempt to read them all; as they are all to the same effect, I shall read one only. I take it that these have been sent by employees of General Motors in Oshawa,, and this particular one reads:
I view with much concern the insecurity of employment in the Canadian automotive industry and therefore urge you to use your influence to bring about an investigation in the industry-in regards to same especially the effect of recent tariff adjustments.
With regard to what the leader of the opposition has said, it is common information that the tariff board has been investigating the automobile industry for some years. May I ask if the present tariff was based on the findings of the tariff board?

I believe I represent a district which manufactures more automobiles than any other district in Canada. Before the minister replies to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) and the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore), may I say that the newspaper article to which the leader of the opposition referred was also sent to me. I have received other communications of apprehension from men engaged in the automobile industry. These have come to me from people who live in the areas where different branches of the automobile industry are located, as well as from other centres in Ontario and the province of Quebec. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) makes his statement, I am sure he will note that those of us who come from the areas concerned have been alive to this problem. We are

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: ' I was wanting to answer the questions that have been asked, but apparently hon. members are associating themselves for the purpose of getting some statement from me. I was trying to answer the specific questions asked by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) and the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore), and I had no intention of closing off the debate on this item. In so far as it intimates that the government of Canada has made representations to the government of the United States since the signing of the treaty, it is entirely incorrect.

The minister means with
reference to automobiles, because this government has made representations with regard to cattle.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The article referred
specifically to automobiles, and there is no foundation in fact for that statement. Another allegation was made that because of the provisions in the treaty two of the three large automobile manufacturers were considering withdrawing from Canada. I have no information which would lead me to believe that there is any truth in that statement.
In reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Ontario, I may say that there has been no report by the tariff board. As my hon. friend knows, the reference with respect to automobiles has been a continuing one and the treaty was negotiated with the United States without the aid, if I may put it in that way, of a final report from the tariff board.

Just before the item carries, in view of the discussion I think some of us might express a word from a

slightly different point of view, because there are other points of view in the house than those which have been placed before the minister.
While we have every sympathy with the men who are engaged in this industry, we cannot be blind to the fact that it has grown up behind what has been in the past a fairly substantial protective tariff; and if the plea were made by the companies more genuinely from the point of view of safeguarding the interests of the men employed in this industry there would be much more sympathy with it.
I have in mind this fact, that in the automobile industry men have worked under conditions which have to a large degree undermined their health; that while rates of wages have looked high when considered on an hourly or daily basis, the yearly wage in the automobile industry has not been, over the years, relatively high; and I have observed in this industry, in the city of Regina where my home is, that when times grew slack men congregated day after day round the doors of the automobile plant hoping for work and were often employed for just a few hours.
It seems to me that if an industry which can pile up dividends, surpluses, reserves and so on to the extent that this industry has done, receives protection from the Dominion of Canada or from any other country, it ought also to be made to assume responsibilities with regard to its working force. I want to place that point of view before the committee, because I have every sympathy with the men whose jobs are in jeopardy; but at the same time I want to make it abundantly clear that over a period of years the people of Canada have paid for automobiles prices far in excess of what should have been paid; and moreover the industry, while it has paid, as I have said, a relatively high hourly or daily wage, has not assumed responsibility for the care and safeguarding of the men whom it has employed.
Hence, when I hear a plea made in this chamber, as it has been this afternoon, apparently wholly from the point of view of those who are likely to lose their jobs in the industry, I come back to the thought that there are other considerations which ought to be reviewed when we are considering protective tariffs, if we are asked to maintain them for this industry.
May I say just a word in reference to what has been said by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar? He has spoken of the high protection accorded to the motor car industry of Canada.

In past years.

Canada-United States Trade Agreement

In past years. I venture to say that for some years Canada has had the second lowest protective rate of any producing country in the world. It must be remembered also that we have a free item, a free import from the United Kingdom, and no other motor-car producing country has a free item.
If the hon. member will think back for just a moment or two, he will recall that it is not only tariff rates which affect employment in and the productivity of an industry; it is changes in rates; and I venture to say that in the last ten or fifteen years there have been not less than a hundred changes made in the tariff rates on the materials and the parts used in the automotive industry of this country. The hon. member will also remember, I hope, that when the United Kingdom was a free trade country, or so called, about 1915, it imposed a tariff rate of some thirty per cent-if I am not wrong- against the motor-cars of the United States, or under its general tariff, giving us a preference of one-third off. The British government did that for a specific purpose. The United Kingdom was not given to protective tariffs at that time; it was not a protective country; it did not believe in the principle of protection. It gave protection to the motorcar industry because of its impregnation of life into other industries, because of its encouragement in the production of alloy steels, and I hope I can have the backing of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) when I say, more particularly because no country to-day can defend itself without the modern armament which comes from the production of flexible power. There are two things tp be considered-and again with deference to the superior knowledge of the Minister of National Defence-in connection with modem armaments. One is the aeroplane, and the aeroplane has developed out of the motor-car engine. The other is the tank, and the tank has developed out of the tractor. And we make no tractors in this country.
We should.

I quite agree that we should. We make no tractors in this country, and we are not encouraging the manufacture in this country of motor-car engines as we should be doing if we wish some day to have a self-respecting position so far as self-defence is concerned.
I wonder if the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, who has a very great regard for workers in this country, is quite right in his
reference to wages. I had occasion some two or three years ago to look up the annual wage drawings of the men in the motor-car industry, and as I recall it, sir, they were about the third or the fourth best-paid employees in Canada.
What year was that?

I should say three or four years ago. We have been dropping back. There was a time when we in this country made twice as many motor-cars as the United Kingdom, and I am speaking offhand when I say that the situation is reversed.
I did not intend to speak on this subject, but I will say this, that the conditions of men in the motor-car industry are terrible. It is not only the men that are on relief; it is the men, as the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar said, that are employed only half-time.
So far as the general argument on the treaty is concerned. I do not propose to enter into it now, but I will say this, that the motor-car industry will be glad to have less than the average rate which has been conceded to agriculture under the agreement. I have gone over it rather carefully, and I find that there are far greater duties in favour of the live stock industry, -I think forty-five per cent under this agreement placed on beef and veal from the United States. There is some sixty or seventy per cent on importations from the Argentine, which is a good customer for some of our manufactured products.
The other day I heard the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) speaking eloquently about the protection which should be given the dairy industry. The motor-car industry will be glad to have just one-half of the consideration which is given to the daily industry in this country.

I will
support that too.

When the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar speaks of the disparity in prices, I would just have him remember that it is an illusion to think that the duty is high on durable goods because you pay it in a bulk sum. You swallow your protection on agricultural production three times a day throughout the year.

Some of our protectionist friends on both sides of the house have joined together in favour of the retention of the excise tax on automobiles. I wish to associate myself with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) in the effort to have the tax taken away. I was very

much surprised indeed, when there was any suggestion on the part of the government of touching either the duty or the excise tax on automobiles, that there was not a roar from the automobile industry. I can remember what happened in 1926. I saw them come here with their labourers, parading in front of the buildings and carrying placards reading, "I have fought for Canada, I have bled for Canada, and now I have to leave Canada because we are going to be thrown out of work." When they were told that the government would stand by the reduction in the duty they went back home, and what did they do? They made their factories bigger and increased the manufacture of automobiles so that production was greater than it had ever been before.
An lion. MEMBER: Export trade.
Yes, but a good deal of it was home trade as well, and the home trade was better immediately after that was done than it had been for many years before.
Will the hon. gentleman tell the committee what budget changes were made subsequently that gave relief?

The duty remained,
and all I know is that when I went to buy an automobile I paid anywhere from $50 or $75 to $100 less. I can see that by the removal of the excise tax people will be able to buy cars still cheaper.

They will pay for
it in increased taxation.

If we pay for it in
some other form I am not concerned with that. The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore) referred to the fact that farmer's had a great deal of protection. Well, so far as the wheat growers of western Canada are concerned, they have no protection in any shape or form. There is a duty on wheat, but that does not do us a particle of good. The duty on wheat, cattle, barley, oats and rye could be removed, and its removal would not mean anything to us. The duty is not a bit of good to us. It is all eye-wash, window-dressing, something to talk about to show that you are protecting the farmer. But such protection is of no use to us. We have to pay duties on the commodities we buy, and we do not get a bit of good from the duty on wheat. You put a duty on vegetables, machinery and other commodities that we use, and we pay.
Are you getting a guaranteed price for your wheat in the west?

We are getting a guaranteed price, yes. And why should we not? We have been contributing for years to the manufacturing concerns, so why should we not get a guaranteed price? I shall discuss that later on, but at the moment I am talking about automobiles and the hon. member will not divert me. Reference was also made to assistance given to dairymen. If you are going to use the dairymen in the way you have used the automobile people, then I suggest that the dairymen should get their cream separators free of duty, because the automobile people get their raw products free.
There is a suggestion that some automobile manufacturers may move out of the country. If any of them have moved or if they intend to move, it is not because they are not getting enough protection; it is because of the regulations and the manner in which the duty is collected. If I live in the west I pay duty not only on the automobile at the factory door, but on the freight as well. If I live in British Columbia I pay duty on about $150 more than I would pay for the car at the factory door because it costs that much more by reason of the freight. That is the first injustice to which the western consumer is subject. We pay duty on the car and on the freight to destination at a point south of the line out there, which is unfair to us and makes the duty that much higher.
Another point is this. These manufacturers hire an importing agent. The agent crosses the line and makes regulations and certain arrangements whereby the cars are bought, not at the retail price but "wholesale, which is twenty-five, thirty and sometimes even as much as forty per cent less than the retail price on the other side; and when they bring the car to this country, if it costs $1,000 they pay duty not on $1,000 but on $650 or $700. Therefore they get a reduction and are able then quite easily to compete with manufacturers of cars in this country.
I maintain that the duty on cars should be collected at the factory door-wherever it may be in the United States-and we should impose that duty on the retail price, not on the wholesale price. The duty could be adjusted so as to be reasonable. But the way in which the duty is collected on automobiles to-day has made it possible for some of the automobile people to cross the line and manufacture in the United States instead of in Canada. That is the trouble; it is not the duty but the manner in which the duty is collected. The regulations should be changed.

Before the discussion takes too wide a range, I should like to refer to some remarks made by the leader of the

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
opposition (Mr. Manion) and two or three other members. The leader of the opposition referred to a dispatch to the Detroit Free Press. I have not seen that dispatch; but as I understood it, it was suggested by the writer that concern was being felt that two or three of the so-called big automobile manufacturing companies might transfer operations from Canada to the United States. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has referred to it, and I want to confirm what he has said. 1 have never heard it suggested that anything of that kind was likely to occur. I have never heard the fear expressed that it might occur. The fear has been expressed that a limited range of cars with small Canadian content might possibly be manufactured on the other side of the line instead of on this side. Whether that fear is justified I am not able to say with certainty; but the suggestion that has been made to me as Minister of National Revenue-and that is probably the reason why my name is mentioned in that regard- is that the law respecting valuations for duty purposes is not being properly applied by the Department of National Revenue. All that I can say in that regard is that these representations are receiving the consideration of the Department of National Revenue at the present time. I do not think there is anything more I can add.

The discussion has taken a much wider range than I had contemplated. Being of a peaceful disposition, I assure the committee that the last thought in the world that entered my mind was to stir up any contention. I really was looking for information, and I have got some; more, I must confess, from my hon. friend to my right and some other hon. gentlemen than from the ministers perhaps, because apparently the article w'as not sent to them. There have been resolutions-[DOT]
One from the city council of Windsor.
Without grousing.

Yes, I do not think there has been much growling from the east. To my mind it has been done in a very fine spirit. When the east is willing to do that, I do not think the antagonistic attitude of the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly)-

They took it from us
before; why should they not give some of it back?

-towards protection in general was altogether justified. After all, if we have kept men at work in Windsor, Oshawa and other cities, it is just as useful to Canada as to keep men at work out west. We should remember that we are working on the basis of a Canadian nation, not just the east or the west. I think some in the east as well as some in the west, but perhaps a greater proportion in the west, must learn that the east and the west must work together.
But if the statements made in this resolution are correct, the danger is that what is going to happen is that two or three big companies in Windsor or Oshawa may close down or reduce their operations so that there will be very much less employment in those cities, and yet automobiles will not be any cheaper. In other words, there will not be any cut in price at all, and thousands of men being thrown out of work will add to the troubles of this country, and of this government if you will.
In regard to the remark of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that these industries should take.care of their men, again I agree with him. I think we are

coming to the time when all industries must do more than they have done in the past to ensure the year-round employment and the future of their employees. It happens rather strangely that I recall speaking to a huge meeting of industrialists in the Prince Edward hotel, in the city of Windsor on October 15, 1931, when I was a minister of the late government-I remember the date for a personal reason of my own-and advocating that very thing. I pointed out that there had been too much tendency in the past-
Will the hon. member permit a question

Will the hon. member first let me finish my sentence. I said there had been too much tendency in the past for industrialists, when conditions became bad, to take care of their plant and machinery but to let the human part of their organization, their employees, the most important part, be turned out on the street to be cared for by charity or by the state. I believe industry must correct that. A good many companies in the United States and some in Canada are to-day doing so. Industry must combine with the government of the day, whatever government it may happen to be, in caring for its employees, giving them work throughout the year so far as it can be done.
Now did my hon. friend wish to ask a question?
I can cover it later.

That is the main point I wanted to make. It is not a case in my mind of trying to care for the shareholder or the bondholder; I am not particularly worried about them; I am chiefly interested in maintaining employment in this country. We have built up the industry, and I believe the government might very well give serious thought to the presentations which have been made here this afternoon from various sections of the house. I do not think they are finished; I know the hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Brown) has been trying a number of times to get an opportunity to speak for his section. Many sections of Canada are affected. I hope the ministers are correct in their statement, although neither of them seems very familiar with the statements made here.

The hon. member for

I referred specifically to the condition of unemployment in so far as it affected the workingmen employed in the automobile industry. On that occasion I pointed out, and I do so again to-day, that the automobile industry, important as it is to the economy of this country, is at the same time illustrative of some of the weaknesses of what I called then and call now our acquisitive and competitive system. Consequently, and assuming that this system is here to stay for some time in spite of what hon. gentlemen opposite may wish, this is a fact. With this in mind, I urge this house and this government to bring in at once a system of contributory unemployment insurance on a national scale, so as to take care of the unemployment in reference to that particular industry.
How could it?

I cannot get on to that point, because I have discussed it already. The automobile industry is certainly one in which that measure would definitely apply.
I think the leader of the opposition did not go perhaps as far as I would when he said that we are now faced with the fact that the automobile industry is here. Whether or not it should have been introduced into our economy is another question, the leader of the opposition observed. Looking at the facts squarely, I suggest to him and to hon. members of this, committee, having in mind all the subsidiary industries that are dependent upon the automobile industry; having in mind the thousands of men directly employed in that industry and in other industries which owe their existence to it, it is a very good thing for Canada that among our secondary industries we have the automobile industry. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), who these days is confronted with the problem of giving men work, would indeed be faced with a tremendous problem if not only in my own city but in Oshawa and other places throughout this country there was no automobile industry.

My hon. friend
suggests that the automobile industry is here to stay. It is here under certain privileges, and I would ask the hon. member whether the government ought not to insist that something like security of employment and decent wages should be maintained.
I fully agree with that. A few moments ago I repeated what I stated in this house when the resolution urging the adoption of a scheme of unemployment insurance was under discussion.
Let the government take the responsibility.
Of course; I have said so, and I repeat it. That is one of the delights of being on this side of the house; one can freely express a dissentient view without fear of the party whip.
As long as you vote right.
The hon. member may be sure I will vote right.
Why should not the industry carry the risk?

I am coming to that, and it is a perfectly proper question. When this government took office in 1935 they did what I thought was the proper thing, having in mind the complex features of this industry; they referred the whole matter to the tariff board, where it remains under a continuing reference. I attended the hearings of that board for almost two and a half months in an endeavour not only to follow the briefs and presentations but also to learn something about an industry of which, as to its technical side, I had very little knowledge. No one who followed that inquiry would dare rise in his place in this house and dogmatically say either that there should be no tariff on automobiles or that there should be an excessive tariff. The man who makes that sort of extreme statement I dare say is not familiar with the problem itself. But while the tariff board has considered and continues to consider this problem, I fully agree with what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said. There is a duty upon industry to provide adequately, to the extent that industry can for its employees who inevitably, even in normal times, are not continuously engaged during the course of the year.

I do not want to appear narrow or sectional in my outlook; I trust that my conduct in this house has been otherwise. But I cannot help agreeing in a measure perhaps not with the provocation but with some of the things suggested by the leader of the opposition. Undoubtedly anyone who looks at our problem generally will be impressed with the need of continued compromise between one section and another. It is not going to do my hon. friends from the west any good to suggest to those of us who live in the east that we are unmindful of the problems of the west or that under our economy we are causing those in the west to be continually subordinated to our interests. Surely that is not the picture. Undoubtedly we have conflicting economic interests, and the task of government in this country is to reconcile and compromise those interests in the interests of all.
I might rise in my place in this house and make myself a very popular man in my own constituency and my own province by saying, "I am going to oppose the wheat bonus. I am going to oppose the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act." I could make myself a very popular member in Windsor and other parts of Ontario if I did that, but I am not going to stoop to that kind of practice. I simply make an appeal to the house, to my hon. friends from the west who have great problems, to realize that we in the east have great problems as well. Come to my own city of Windsor; go up street after street and you will find men and women living under the most difficult economic circumstances, just as difficult as those experienced by the unfortunate people in the drought areas of the west. And what is true in the urban part of my riding is equally true in the rural section. We too have our problems, and we are not going to get anywhere in this house by pitting our sectional and political interests against the interests of Canada generally.
I hope I have not spoken too strongly, but I do feel that hon. members and particularly those from the western part of this country, regardless of their political affiliations, should realize what the automobile industry means to Canada. True, as a consumer, the western farmer is placed under a difficulty to which, with a freer system of trade, he would not be subjected; but that is an inevitable circumstance in the economy of this country, as long as we are going to preserve under this confederation nine provinces, with these various sectional interests; and the sooner we realize this, the better.
The leader of the opposition has referred to the resolution which was passed by the city council of Windsor. I forwarded that

That resolution represents a perfectly legitimate concern. Mr. Chairman, it is not customary to start in on a new schedule without the minister making a general statement covering the whole schedule. In the agreement as it is before us, there is a summary preceding schedule II, but surely on an important matter such as this the minister will make a general statement. We have another minister handling this part of the agreement, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), and it is only reasonable to expect from him a general statement in like manner as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) made a statement. I have never in all my experience in this house seen the committee of ways and means start on a schedule just as fast as we have started on this, by the chairman calling item 1, without any statement whatsoever from the minister. If the minister is not quite clear as to the sort of statement we expect, it might assist him if I asked a few questions.
Has the minister been in close collaboration with his colleagues on every item of this section, or did one minister give certain concessions in the Canadian market without a correlated study by the minister directly concerned with concessions received ,by Canada? Is there any balance-sheet based on trade over any given period, whether that trade be trade as shown in the statistics of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the year ending December, 1937, or trade as reflected in the trade statistics as we receive them from our own bureau of statistics?
The minister might also tell us what sort of balance sheet he had in his mind. He is more or less a trained man who, when he looks at a business transaction apart from political considerations, would first give some thought to what we are getting and what we are giving.
I have a full realization, Mr. Chairman, of all the political and other considerations which the minister finds it necessary to carry in his mind, of the good that treaties of this kind may do when negotiated between two democratic countries like Canada and the United States, so closely associated in so many ways, and also of the cooperation that we gave to help the mother country make a trade agreement with the United States. I have all that in mind, but there is another

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
feature, and that is the cold-blooded figures of the balance sheet. That is what we do not have, and I say to this government that they have not been entirely fair to the Canadian people.
I say to the members of this house: You do not know what you are passing in this agreement in dollars and cents. I will put it the other way: Leave out everything else, and I ask, do you know what you are passing in dollars and cents? Have you the information in front of you? Do you not agree with me, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, with all the assistants and executives he has around him, is the man who should be charged with the responsibility of letting us know what we are doing here?
Give us a chance.

It is true he made a speech in the house on the trade treaties in the month of January. 1939, when he apologized because he had only forty minutes and all that sort of thing. But this trade treaty is not limited to the month of January, 1939, and in all fairness to those of us who are at least trying to gather some sort of idea whether this trade treaty is fair and equitable, we should have more information.
In the very document which the Prime Minister tabled on the day these trade treaties were introduced, there was a tabular statement. That tabular statement should have been in our hands six or eight weeks before that. My second observation is this, that that tabular statement, as the minister well knows, when it comes to the concessions which the United States gives to Canada, gives the dollar value of the commodity affected. There is, on the other hand, no similar tabular statement given us by this government as to the amount of goods affected during any particular period by the concessions given by Canada. Why should those of us who are interested in this have to work out the calculation for ourselves, and then not know how the treaties were negotiated? This is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce received for Canada; these are the concessions, taken off as accurately as they could be by clerks and a couple of boys at the university of Toronto who have taken postgraduate courses in commerce and finance and have no political ends to serve. On all items over $25,000, based on the trade of Canada for the year ending March 31, 1938, we have given concessions double in dollar value what we are receiving. That is without
touching excise tax; when excise tax is added, our concessions are treble what we have received.
I complain about this procedure, Mr. Chairman, that you call item No. 1, and the minister is going to slip these items through one after the other, while we who in this House of Commons are charged with responsibility to the Canadian people are not clear as to what we are doing on the hard basis of dollars and cents. The minister has made clear his sentiments about negotiating this deal on behalf of democracy and all that sort of thing, but do we know what we are entitled to know? Has the government, in following the old procedure of holding back information to the very last minute, acted quite fairly towards us? They held back the treaty until it was signed and then gave their press releases. Take this so-called tabular statement of tariff changes; why is this information held back until the matter is introduced in the house and the minister takes his place in this chamber to pass the individual items? That is not giving us a fair opportunity to study this treaty.
Our good friend the United States, as is well known, do not do business in that way. They treat these business matters on a business basis, and I think it is time-never mind the past, "it was done this way before," and all that sort of thing-we had a little more business principle injected into the procedure in this chamber, particularly when we have a problem of this kind, which it is so easy to put in the form of dollars and cents so that he who runs may read. Yet we have not the facts in that particular form.
I am sorry that I have to ask the minister all these questions. I should have liked to see him give the committee a statement and avoid the necessity of asking for this information; but in the absence of it I feel, upon my responsibility as a member of this house, that before the minister goes on with the items, I must ask him to give us some idea as to how they were negotiated, tell us why the less amount of duties payable on goods going into the United States is $2,400,000, while the less amount of duties payable on goods coming into Canada is $5,130,000 and the less amount of excise payable on goods coming into Canada will be anywhere from ten to fifteen million dollars; why on the one hand we should give away from our exchequer some fifteen million dollars, and why on the other the concessions made by the United States amount to only two and a half million dollars. At the same time he should have taken us into his confidence and told

As I said in my remarks yesterday, I stayed away from here for two days on account of the government placing the Minister of Finance in the position of putting this particular measure through the house.

I do not propose to take refuge behind anything that the Minister of Finance may or may not have done. My hon. friend speaks of the minister slipping these items through. There is no intention on the part of the minister, even if he could, to do anything of the kind. I reiterate that it seems to me that now, since we are in committee, we ought to discuss this item by item. My hon. friend has asked 
for a sort of balance sheet or a statement of debits and credits as to the amount of business affected in our imports and our exports. I think all that was pretty well dealt with; but if he is going to expect me to say that, when one particular item was negotiated with United States representatives, we would then say, "Now we are going to get so much on this item and we are going to give so much on the other item" and try to strike an absolute balance, I am sure that every intelligent man in the house-and they are all intelligent-must know that such is absolutely impossible.
All intelligent except me, I suppose.

I wish to ask this question regarding this item and all others. Was there any consultation with business or labour or agriculture before this change was entered into? It seems to me the change is for the benefit of the United States. Did the minister do what was done at Washington? There they consulted industry, labour, business and agriculture and gave them a chance. I submit that when we are dealing with something of this great importance and magnitude, those who are affected have a right to be heard. What steps did the minister take to notify the Canadian interests I name, concerned? At Washington they had thirty days in which to file objections and three months to appear before a board. Even admitting the difference in constitution and functions between the two governments, surely in a matter of this magnitude, before such far-reaching hundreds and hundreds of changes are brought about, those who are vitally affected should be consulted.

No.

What I have to say on
this item has reference generally to the whole treaty. My remarks can be applied to this particular item, and I put them forward as a suggestion, and a hope that in future trade agreements we may avoid the discussion that has taken place here to-night. The question has been asked, to what extent the people interested in this particular item were consulted? Were they given an opportunity to make representations? Were they advised that this item was one which was under consideration, as happened in the United States? When the people on the United States side of the line are drawing up a treaty of this kind or entering into negotiations, as the minister well knows, every item in their part of the treaty that is going to be affected was discussed with those interested, and the people manufacturing the product in the United States, or who might be directly or indirectly affected, were consulted long before the people representing Canada were negotiating with the government of the United States. I have in my hand an extract from volume 48, part 1, Public Laws of the United States, 1933-34, with particular reference to the Tariff Act of 1930 amendment approved June 12, 1934 -it even gives the time of approval, 9.15 p.m. I read section 4:
Before any foreign trade agreement is concluded with any foreign government or instrumentality thereof under the provisions of this act, reasonable public notice of the intention to negotiate an agreement with such government or instrumentality shall be given in order that any interested person may have an opportunity to present his views to the President or to such agency as the President may designate, under such rules and regulations as the President may prescribe; and before concluding such agreement the President shall seek information and advice in respect thereto from the United States tariff commission, the Departments of State, Agriculture and Commerce and such other sources as he may deem appropriate.
So we see that the negotiators on the part of the United States are carefully circumscribed by certain provisions that prevent their industries from being injured without fair opportunity being given to make representation beforehand in proper quarters. In other words, those negotiating the treaty for the United States are better armed than those negotiating the treaty on behalf of Canada. 
In particular reference to this item 1, and with reference generally to all items in this treaty, I claim and maintain that those interested in the various items in Canada were not given the same opportunity as those in the United States, and I am asking the government to give consideration to the possibility of incorporating into our law what they have in the laws of the United States, something that will give our people a better opportunity to make their views known to the government long before the terms of a treaty are negotiated and signed and come into effect. I think that is a fair and reasonable suggestion, it is a proposition that I have urged on previous occasions and one which I think should commend itself to every hon. member, as it certainly does to everyone engaged in business and industry in Canada.

I should like to ask
the minister a couple of simple questions in order to get this clear in my mind. Yes, it is described as imports.
From all countries?

Yes, and then there is a column headed "From Canada"; one column for the total imports and the other for imports from Canada.

I could understand his argument. But this is a case where we are obtaining advantages for Canadian producers in the United States market. We are trying to do something for these people. This was done at the request of the Canadian producers. We tried to please them and I think we have helped. I do not see how anyone could possibly be injured as my hon. friend charges. As the minister knows, this lumber bargain is the only part of the whole trade treaty which has not yet been concluded by both parties, and I think our government might have some effect on the United States government if they pointed out the unfairness of leaving the lumber bargain in the first stage, where it is at the present time.
In this first stage Canada has made certain concessions. I do not intend to enumerate them in detail, but roughly-I would ask the minister to correct me if I am wrong-they are that we have given up a portion of our preference in the United Kingdom and in the West Indies; we have agreed to give up a portion of our preference in Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, and we have reduced the duty on dressed lumber coming into Canada from United States by fifty per cent, as well as taking off the excise tax. I do not think it can be argued successfully that Canada has got fair compensation for those concessions in this first stage of the lumber bargain. Further than that, these concessions have been made almost exclusively by the British Columbia lumbermen. The concessions do not affect the eastern lumbermen, but they do affect, and vitally so, the lumbermen on the Pacific coast.
Then, in the second stage we have to make further concessions, and I believe that in that stage as well British Columbia is doing most of the sacrificing. But because of the unfairness of the first stage, I earnestly ask the minister to have the government press the government of the United States to bring about the second stage by removing the import excise tax of $1.50 a thousand feet. Just this week I received the current copy, March, 1939, of the British Columbia Lumberman, which is the journal of the trade. On page 35 I find an article dealing with this lumber situation. I should like to read the

In other words, we in British Columbia are asking that the second stage be brought into force so that our lumber may get into the United States market and thereby make this deal fair to both.
