Under this treaty you can now get $6.60 per 100 pounds for a decent steer, from seven to seven and a half and eight cents a pound if it is a good one, compared with three and three and a half cents down to a cent and a quarter and a cent and a half a pound in 1932 and 1933. Those were the black days. Although we managed to get through somehow, those were days which left many of our farmers in a situation from which they never recovered. Certainly I should hate to think that my relatives in Lanark county would be worried respecting this trade agreement, which certainly will prove, and undoubtedly up to date has proven of immense value to them as farmers.

Every time that the hon. member for Renfrew North rises in his place in this chamber he takes a whack at me. I do not blame him a bit, because I spent two weeks in Renfrew North trying to lick him, and if it had not been that the election was on the fifth of April, that the roads were impassable, and the day was one of the worst that ever came, he would not be sitting in this house. I do not intend to follow his argument, because I never heard so much nonsense talked in as short a space of time. He has told us about calves and dairy cows. Mr. Chairman, you know that the tariff respecting them has not been changed; it is the same as it was since 1935, and we never filled our quota. As we have not filled our quota with calves, enlarging the quota cannot mean anything to our farmers; there was no advantage to them in having it raised, and no change has occurred under it. I am sorry that the

Dear Sir:
Regarding shipments of cattle to the United States of America during the first quarterly quota, when as you know that nearly half of that quota was filled 'by Mexican cattle, thus working a hardship on the shipper from Canada, also very costly on the shipper who had his cattle en route when this quota was filled as there was no warning-just filled.

Don't you think some adjustment should be made to the shipper that had his cattle en route when this quota was filled in this way? It has meant between $350 to $400 a car through absolutely no fault of ours. In my case it amounts to $361. Why should we have to lose this through not proper protection of our share of the quota? In this we can hardly take this loss.
All I wish -to say in this connection is that I believe the hon. member for Portage la Prairie has made many valuable suggestions to the minister, and I should like to add my voice to his in suggesting to the minister that the three month period be narrowed down to perhaps either two months or one month.

Upon what date was
the notice given that ten per cent still remained, and upon what date did the quota end?
The quota ended early in February-February 2, I think.
On what date was the notice given that ten per cent remained?

I cannot tell the hon. member that. I do not know. I might make this observation, that the difficulty which arose in the first quarter was rather because of an abnormal condition. It was not anticipated that Mexico would send such a large quantity of cattle into the United States in that quarter, 71492-140
and it was for that reason that the surplus of cattle en route to the United States was so large. In order to provide against that in the future-and I think perhaps it will be provided against in this way-we are receiving early in the quarter, I believe about every four weeks, notice from the United States government as to how many cattle have been admitted; then later on, when we get nearer to the end of the quarter and the quota is nearer to the point of exhaustion, we receive notice by telegram, and that is communicated to the stock-yards and to the Commercial Intelligence Journal and by other means to the exporters in Canada so that they can govern themselves accordingly.

Is it not a fact that the trouble really arose because notification that only ten per cent remained of the quota was given just a few days before the quota was filled? I have had letters similar to the one which has just been read.
I think the real reason was the unexpected supply from Mexico.

Personally I think the market in the United States for our meats has been of uncertain value for many years. The preference that is extended to the United States producer in this line is similar to the preference extended in many other directions. It will not only give the United States producer a place in the greatest market of the world but surrender again stability in markets that we have been long endeavouring to establish.
We have had a haphazard market in the United States, a very uncertain market. There was an over-supply. Our exports of live stock to the United States were insignificant even in 1930. Take the year 1921, if you want to compare different years-and I am not charging this to the government that is in power to-day, because it was the trend of development. We shipped more live stock to the markets of the world in 1921 than we have done since. Our export market for bacon had practically disappeared between 1921 and 1930, Denmark having captured that market from us in the old land. In 1921 we sold twice as many cattle to the United States as the whole global quota includes now-in cattle and calves, upwards of half a million. But the Fordney-McCumber tariff closed us out over-night and we were left for years not knowing what to do with our surplus live stock. In 1929 we had recovered the market to some extent, but the Hawley-Smoot tariff closed us out again. Now we have a temporary advantage in that uncertain market for some of these products, but we have cut the tariff in this item from two cents to one cent-
